passage.bullet: Deep limestone caves like Creswell Crags → shielded Palaeolithic families from freezing Ice Age winds
Knapping flint into tear-drop handaxes → let makers chop meat and firewood without metal
Team hunts for woolly mammoths → supplied meat, warm fur hides, bone, and lamp fat

context.bullet: Zero written records in prehistory → footprints at Happisburgh prove families walked Norfolk mud
No farms or shops existed → families had to follow wild herds across icy land

stems.stem: During the freezing Ice Age, Old Stone Age families survived harsh weather by sheltering inside deep ____________ such as ____________.
Since nobody had metal yet, makers chipped ____________ flakes to shape sharp ____________ for chopping meat and wood.
Tracking giant ____________ together gave families vital meat, warm ____________, bones, and fat for lamps.

lesson_1.watch_out: Old Stone Age humans never hunted dinosaurs—dinosaurs died out millions of years before Happisburgh footprints or woolly mammoths.

passage.bullet: Spreading green forests → brought red deer, wild boar, berries, and hazelnuts to hunt and gather
Small hunter-gatherer groups moved each season → followed river fish and ripening woodland plants
Star Carr builders laid wooden platforms → carved red-deer antler headdresses for disguises or dances

context.bullet: Giant woolly mammoths disappeared as ice melted → hunters tracked smaller, faster woodland prey instead
Cheddar Man from Gough's Cave → DNA revealed dark skin, dark curls, and blue eyes

stems.stem: Once the ice melted after 10,000 BC, spreading ____________ brought animals like ____________ and wild boar plus hazelnuts.
Instead of staying in one village all year, Mesolithic ____________ moved camp each season to fish rivers and pick ____________.
Beside a Yorkshire lake at ____________, families built wooden ____________ and carved antler ____________ for disguises or dances.

lesson_1.watch_out: Mesolithic families at Star Carr built wooden platforms, yet they still moved camp seasonally rather than farming all year.

passage.bullet: Low, marshy Doggerland once joined Britain to Europe → families walked across dry land
Warming northern ice sheets poured water into seas → rising waves and storms drowned Doggerland
North Sea trawlers still snag flint tools and mammoth teeth → proves sunken land held camps

context.bullet: Doggerland rivers teemed with eels, ducks, and beavers → rich hunting grounds vanished underwater
Cut off by deep sea water → later newcomers had to sail wooden boats to Britain

stems.stem: For thousands of years before 6500 BC, Doggerland joined Britain to ____________, letting families camp by marshes to catch ____________.
Huge amounts of water from melting northern ____________ poured into the sea until storms drowned the low marshes forever.
Today, fishing boats in the ____________ still pull up ancient ____________ and mammoth teeth from the seabed.

lesson_1.watch_out: Britain was not always an island—until melting ice flooded Doggerland around 6500 BC, people walked straight across from Europe.

passage.bullet: Settlers sailed over with sheep, pigs, cattle, wheat, and barley → began Neolithic British farming
Polished stone axes cleared thick woods while flint sickles reaped grain → created open crop fields
Reliable harvests and coiled clay cooking pots → let families settle in thatched villages all year

context.bullet: Flooded Doggerland made Britain an island → pioneer farmers had to bring livestock on wooden boats
Unlike Mesolithic nomads moving camp each season → Neolithic farmers grew food beside permanent homes

stems.stem: Around 4000 BC, newcomers crossed the sea in ____________ bringing tame animals like ____________ alongside wheat and barley seeds.
Villagers felled thick forests with smooth ____________ and cut ripe crop stalks using curved ____________.
Coiling clay ____________ for hot stews and growing steady harvests let families live in ____________ all year.

lesson_2.watch_out: Neolithic still means New Stone Age—these early farmers cleared forests with polished stone axes, not bronze or iron tools.

passage.bullet: Stacked flat Orkney flagstones → formed eight snug homes linked together by roofed stone passages
Central cooking hearths and stone box beds → kept villagers cosy under heather and sheepskins
Carved stone dressers displayed treasures while indoor drains → carried waste away cleanly

context.bullet: Few trees grew on Orkney → builders used coastal stone slabs instead of timber walls
Deep sand buried Skara Brae for millennia → preserved furniture that rotted in mainland wooden villages

stems.stem: Because windy ____________ had very few trees, villagers around 3100 BC stacked flat ____________ into eight linked homes.
Beneath the sand dunes, diggers found ____________ once stuffed with heather, plus a central ____________ for cooking.
Each snug house even featured a ____________ for showing treasures and indoor stone ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: Skara Brae families were not rough cave dwellers—their linked homes had stone dressers, central hearths, cosy beds, and indoor drains.

passage.bullet: Five dark stone chambers inside the chalk mound → held the bones of nearly fifty ancestors
Mourners left clay bowls, beads, and bone pins → communities gathered outside to share feasts
Giant hilltop barrows stood visible for miles → showed rivals that settled families belonged there

context.bullet: Stored grain harvests fed big work teams → settled villagers could raise huge chalk mounds
Keeping ancestors near village fields → deepened family roots compared with wandering Ice Age hunters

stems.stem: Raised on a Wiltshire hill around 3650 BC, this long mound hid five dark ____________ behind heavy boulders.
Villagers placed the bones of nearly fifty ____________ inside alongside hand-coiled ____________ and beads.
Sharing ____________ outside a giant hilltop tomb proved to everyone that the farming community ____________ to that land.

lesson_2.watch_out: West Kennet Long Barrow was not a tomb for one lone king—villagers placed nearly fifty community ancestors inside over generations.

passage.bullet: Antler picks and bone shovels → dug a circular chalk henge for cremated ancestors
Eighty spotted bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales → 140 miles from Wiltshire
Plant ropes and wooden sledges → let huge teams drag Welsh stones across hills and rivers

context.bullet: Metal tools had not reached Britain in 3000 BC → diggers relied on tough animal bones
Burying cremated dead inside the early chalk ring → continued Neolithic ancestor worship from long barrows

stems.stem: Around 3000 BC on Salisbury Plain, workers chipped a circular ditch using ____________ picks and cattle ____________.
Five centuries later, eighty spotted bluestones were hauled from the ____________ in ____________, roughly ____________ miles away.
Moving those heavy stones across hills and rivers took woven ____________, wooden ____________, and huge teamwork.

lesson_3.watch_out: Stonehenge was not built all at once—it began around 3000 BC as a chalk ditch and cremation ground before big stones arrived.

passage.bullet: Teams hauled grey sarsen boulders twenty miles on wooden sledges and rollers → pounded them smooth
Mortise-and-tenon peg joints → locked heavy lintels onto upright pairs so trilithons never slipped
Chalk houses two miles away at Durrington Walls → sheltered workers sharing huge winter pork feasts

context.bullet: Wooden wheels arrived centuries later in the Bronze Age → Neolithic teams used log rollers instead
Carpenters already joined house timbers with pegs → masons copied those joints onto giant sarsen blocks

stems.stem: Without wheels or cranes, crews pulled massive grey blocks twenty miles on ____________ and log ____________.
To stop top lintels sliding off the uprights, masons carved snug ____________ peg joints.
Two miles away inside warm chalk homes at Durrington Walls, builders shared huge feasts of roast ____________ and ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Top lintel stones were not simply balanced loose on uprights—masons carved snug mortise-and-tenon peg joints just like woodwork.

passage.bullet: Midsummer solstice sunrise shines straight over the Heel Stone → marks the year's longest day
Midwinter solstice sunset glows through the tallest trilithon → promises longer, warmer days will return
Exact sun alignments turned the stone circle into a giant solar calendar and ancestor temple

context.bullet: Tracking summer and winter turning points → helped Neolithic farmers time planting, harvests, and gatherings
Roast pork feasts at Durrington Walls happened in midwinter → matches the winter sunset alignment

stems.stem: On the ____________ solstice, the rising sun shines straight over the Heel Stone into the stone circle.
Six months later at the ____________ solstice, the setting sun glows right between the tallest ____________.
Lining the stones up with the sky gave farming communities both a giant ____________ and an ____________ shrine.

lesson_3.watch_out: Celtic Druids did not build Stonehenge—Neolithic farmers aligned it with the solstice sun roughly two thousand years before Iron Age Druids.

passage.bullet: Beaker newcomers sailed over with comb-stamped clay cups and metalworking know-how → ended Britain's Stone Age
Miners dug green copper inside Great Orme tunnels while Cornish workers gathered heavy tin ore
Smiths crushed ore rock and smelted it over roaring fires → melted pure metal free

context.bullet: Stone Age makers could only chip solid flint → smelting let smiths pour new shapes
Copper lay in North Wales and tin in Cornwall → sparked long-distance British trade routes

stems.stem: Sailing from Europe around 2400 BC, the ____________ people brought bell-shaped pots and Britain's first metal skills.
Underground miners at ____________ in Wales dug green ____________, while workers in ____________ gathered heavy tin.
Crushing the rock and ____________ it over hot fires melted the liquid metal free.

lesson_4.watch_out: Bronze was never dug straight out of the ground ready-made—miners had to find separate copper and tin ores in Wales and Cornwall.

passage.bullet: Pure copper bent easily → mixing nine parts copper with one part tin made tough bronze
Snapped flint stayed ruined forever → broken bronze axes melted down inside stone two-piece moulds
Sharp bronze axes felled thick woodland faster for crops → families guarding metal routes grew rich

context.bullet: Grinding one Neolithic stone axe took days → stone moulds cast identical bronze blades rapidly
Faster forest clearance opened bigger sunny fields → fed growing Bronze Age villages across Britain

stems.stem: Because pure copper bent against hard oak, smiths mixed ____________ parts copper with one part ____________.
Unlike snapped flint, a broken bronze blade could be melted down and recast inside hollow stone ____________.
Tough bronze axes cleared thick ____________ much faster for crops, while families guarding ____________ grew rich.

lesson_4.watch_out: Pure copper alone was too soft for heavy woodcutting—smiths had to alloy copper with Cornish tin to cast hard-wearing bronze.

passage.bullet: Dazzling sheet-gold treasures like the Mold Gold Cape → showed off powerful Bronze Age leaders
Over a hundred grave goods beside the Amesbury Archer → included beakers, copper knives, and gold
Chemical tests on the Archer's tooth enamel → proved he grew up near the snowy Alps

context.bullet: Unlike shared Neolithic ancestor tombs → rich single graves celebrated powerful individual Bronze Age rulers
An Alpine metalworker buried near Stonehenge → proves people and skills travelled right across Europe

stems.stem: Master smiths hammered thin gold into treasures like the Welsh ____________ and crescent-moon ____________ collars for leaders.
Buried around 2300 BC with over a hundred items, the Amesbury grave held five clay ____________ and ____________ knives.
Chemical tests on his ____________ proved this wealthy newcomer had grown up near the snowy ____________.

lesson_4.watch_out: The Amesbury Archer was not born in Wiltshire—tooth enamel chemistry proved he grew up in central Europe near the Alps.

passage.bullet: Cambridgeshire families built thatched wooden roundhouses on oak stilts → stood right above a slow river
Flames swept through the village around 900 BC → families escaped while burning homes plunged downwards
Thick waterlogged mud sealed every fallen object from air → froze daily life like Roman Pompeii

context.bullet: Nearby Flag Fen builders drove thousands of wooden posts → carried a causeway across wet marshes
Just like sand saved Skara Brae → wet mud stopped Must Farm wood from rotting

stems.stem: Around 900 BC in Cambridgeshire, families raised thatched wooden ____________ on sturdy oak ____________ above a slow river.
When a sudden ____________ swept across the roofs, villagers escaped safely as burning homes dropped into the water.
Thick, airless ____________ mud sealed the fallen belongings inside, preserving a snapshot of Bronze Age life.

lesson_5.watch_out: No volcano erupted in Cambridgeshire—thick waterlogged river mud, not volcanic ash, preserved Must Farm after a sudden house fire.

passage.bullet: Clay bowls holding charred porridge and a wooden spoon → showed families fled mid-meal
Fine plant-fibre cloth, willow eel traps, and hafted bronze axes → proved skilled home crafts
Complete one-metre wheel made of ash planks → oldest whole wooden wheel ever found in Britain

context.bullet: Wood, cloth, and food rot away in dry soil → usually only stone or metal survives
Stonehenge builders dragged stones on rollers → Must Farm's ash wheel transformed later heavy transport

stems.stem: Diggers uncovered clay bowls still holding ____________ with a wooden ____________ resting inside.
Rare organic finds included woven wicker ____________ for catching fish and finely spun ____________ cloth.
Built from ash planks around 900 BC, a complete one-metre ____________ became the oldest whole example found in Britain.

lesson_5.watch_out: Bronze Age clothing was not rough animal fur—Must Farm's wet mud preserved finely spun, woven plant-fibre textiles.

passage.bullet: Builders stitched thick oak planks with twisted yew branches → sealed seams tight using soft moss
Crews paddled the Dover sewn-plank boat to France → carried Cornish tin and British bronze
Mediterranean glass beads found at Must Farm → proved British rivers linked into distant trade webs

context.bullet: Flag Fen villagers lowered shiny bronze swords and shields into marshes → honoured sacred waters
Iron nails had not been invented yet → clever plant lashings held sea-going hulls together

stems.stem: Before iron nails existed, Dover builders stitched thick ____________ planks together using twisted ____________ branches and moss.
Paddling between Britain and ____________, crews traded heavy metals such as ____________ and bronze.
Tiny ____________ crafted in ____________ workshops reached Cambridgeshire along long trade routes.

lesson_5.watch_out: The Dover Bronze Age Boat used zero metal nails—shipwrights stitched thick oak planks with twisted yew withies and moss caulking.

passage.bullet: Reddish iron ore lay across hills and bogs → blacksmiths hammered tough saws, swords, and ploughshares
Iron ploughshares sliced heavy clay soil while rotary querns → ground bumper wheat harvests into flour
Thatched roundhouses with wattle-and-daub walls → sheltered families weaving bright wool on upright looms

context.bullet: Unlike rare Cornish tin and Welsh copper → widespread iron ore gave ordinary farmers metal tools
Farming tough clay valleys boosted food supplies → Iron Age villages and tribes grew rapidly

stems.stem: Heating common reddish ____________ in clay furnaces allowed ____________ to hammer strong saws and swords.
Tough iron ____________ sliced heavy clay soil, and families spun stone ____________ to grind grain into flour.
Inside thatched homes built with ____________ walls, villagers wove bright wool on upright ____________.

lesson_6.watch_out: Iron was not cast in stone moulds like bronze—blacksmiths had to heat red-hot iron and hammer it into shape.

passage.bullet: Growing populations sparked rivalry for cattle and farmland → tribes fortified high ridges for safety
Wave-like chalk ramparts and winding gates at Maiden Castle → trapped raiders beneath slingshot fire
Storage pits and iron forges inside the banks → protected tribal grain harvests and smiths

context.bullet: Iron ploughs created rich wheat stores and big herds → gave rival warriors tempting prizes
Oxfordshire tribes carved the giant Uffington White Horse → marked proud tribal territory across miles

stems.stem: As Britain's population grew, competing groups clashed over prized ____________ and fertile ____________.
At Dorset's ____________, huge chalk ____________ and winding entrances slowed raiders facing river ____________ stones.
Inside the high banks, villagers stored winter ____________ in pits and forged red-hot ____________.

lesson_6.watch_out: Maiden Castle was not a medieval stone castle—Iron Age hillforts used giant earth and chalk ramparts, deep ditches, and timber gates.

passage.bullet: Twisted neck rings like the Snettisham Great Torc → proved Celtic smiths mastered fine goldwork
Horse-stamped gold stater coins → showed wealthy British rulers traded across the sea with Rome
Emperor Claudius sent four Roman legions in AD 43 → brought written records that ended prehistory

context.bullet: Druids memorised laws while Thames bronze shields → continued ancient water offerings seen at Flag Fen
From Happisburgh flint knappers to coin-minting kingdoms → Britons built complex societies long before Romans arrived

stems.stem: Twisted neck rings such as the ____________ alongside bronze shields offered to the ____________ prove skilled artistry.
By 50 BC, rulers stamped horses onto ____________ and traded across the water with ____________ and Rome.
When ____________ sent four invading ____________ in AD 43, written records ended British prehistory.

lesson_6.watch_out: Iron Age Britons were not backward savages—before Claudius invaded in AD 43, tribes minted gold coins, forged fine torcs, and traded overseas.
